subject: RFI: Workload traffic slices and GPU class mapping for reserved inference capacity
messages:
From: Orion AI - Procurement <procurement@orionai.com>
To: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-05-18T09:14:00-07:00
Subject: RFI: workload slicing and GPU mapping for reserved capacity

Hi Dev,

Thanks for agreeing to take our RFI. Attached is a short questionnaire (orion_rfi_questions.pdf) focused on reserved inference capacity. Our buying team needs a clear mapping from our workload classes to recommended GPU families, expected throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec), and a sample reservation sizing plan that includes headroom for burst windows.

High level context:
- Orion runs conversational assistants (multi-turn chat), document embeddings (batch), and re-ranking pipelines (low-latency).
- Monthly token volume estimate: ~4B tokens, with peak 1-hour burst at ~10x baseline.
- Latency SLOs: chat P50 < 120ms, P95 < 450ms for 16k context models; embeddings batch can tolerate higher latency.

Can you provide recommended GPU classes (e.g., H100, A100, L4), sizing examples for a 12-month reserved pool (including autoscale/burst strategy), and any guidance on quantization/throughput tradeoffs? Also note any constraints on model variants and fallback behaviors.

Appreciate a short worksheet or workbook so we can validate numbers.

Regards,
Alice Gomez
Orion AI - Procurement
From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>
To: Alice Gomez <alice.gomez@orionai.com>, Orion AI - Procurement <procurement@orionai.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-05-18T13:28:00-07:00
Subject: Re: RFI: workload slicing and GPU mapping for reserved capacity

Hi Alice,

Thanks — attaching a starter workbook (reserved_capacity_workbook.xlsx) and a short answers PDF. Below is a concise mapping and the assumptions we used. I kept the dataset high-level so your engineering team can validate with sample traffic. If you'd like, we can run a quick 60-minute workshop to walk through a live sizing exercise.

Executive summary (short):
- Chat / interactive (low latency, multi-turn): H100-80 or A100-80 strongly recommended for 16k+ context models. If cost pressure, quantized A100-40/80 variants with Redwood Optimize profiles provide 1.6–2.1x cost savings at modest latency impact.
- Embeddings (batch, high throughput): L4-class or A10-class GPUs with 4-bit/8-bit quantized kernels give the best $/embedding at scale. Use batching windows to increase throughput and lower unit cost.
- Re-ranking / short text inference (strict P95): A100-80 in pinned pools with pre-warmed KV cache; or mixed-pool strategy where hot paths route to H100.

Key throughput benchmarks (representative; measured on our runtime with your typical prompt shapes):
- 7B chat model (quantized int8) on L4: ~1.2k tokens/sec per GPU (batched, embeddings use larger batch sizes).
- 70B chat model (A100-80, optimized kernels): ~850 tokens/sec per GPU single-stream; with continuous batching and 8-concurrency it yields ~6.8k tokens/sec effective.
- 1B embedding model (L4, fp16->int8): ~18k embeddings/sec per GPU at batch size 512.
- Re-ranker (cross-encoder 220M) on A100-40: ~2.4k requests/sec (single-token outputs).

Sample 12-month reservation blueprint (starting point):
- Baseline committed pool: 8 x A100-80 GPUs (handles steady-state conversational load ~120 qps equivalent with caching and batching).
- Burst lane (shared): 16 x L4 for embeddings/batch jobs and overflow for less latency-sensitive chat.
- Hot lane (reserved, premium SLA): 4 x H100-80 for low-latency P95-sensitive slices (can be autoscaled up during launches).
- Autoscale policy: allow burst up to 3x baseline for hourly events using pre-approved burst credits; fall back to quantized variants if high-priority hot lane saturates.

Operational considerations:
- Prefix/KV caching reduces required GPU counts by ~20–40% for multi-turn chat depending on prompt reuse. We recommend enabling prefix caching for all chat endpoints with >30% repetition in session turns.
- Continuous batching (default on Redwood) will improve throughput; tunes depend on your latency SLOs.
- Model variants & fallback: Redwood supports policy-based routing — you can pin a model version to the reserved pool, and have automatic fallback to quantized or lower-capacity variants in other regions/pools during saturation.

Open questions for you (so our workbook can be precise):
1) Typical prompt+response token distribution (we used 300 in / 250 out as default).
2) Target steady-state RPS per workload slice (chat vs embeddings vs re-rank).
3) Expected frequency and duration of peak bursts (1-hour, 4-hour?).

I'll follow up with a PDF summarizing these numbers and a workbook you can open.

Thanks,
Dev Patel
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Hi Dev,

Helpful — thanks. A few follow-ups from the infra and procurement teams:

- For tail latency: can you share P95 and P99 numbers for the 70B chat model on A100-80 with and without prefix caching at 1.5x and 3x baseline load?
- Cost/throughput tradeoff: can we get rough $/1M tokens for the configurations (hot lane H100, A100-80 quantized, and L4 batch)?
- Reservation mechanics: do burst credits incur a separate metered bill or are they included in the reservation terms? Also want to know about guaranteed capacity during regional outages and cross-region failover behavior.

We can provide prompt distribution shortly — baseline is closer to 220 tokens in / 180 tokens out; bursts are typically 60–90 minutes during product demos and marketing events.

Thanks,
Alice
From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: RFI: workload slicing and GPU mapping for reserved capacity

Alice — good questions, answered inline and attached a short benchmark PDF (throughput_benchmarks.pdf).

1) Tail latency (70B chat on A100-80):
- Steady-state (1.0x baseline): P95 ~ 320ms, P99 ~ 640ms (with prefix caching enabled P95 drops to ~220ms, P99 to ~480ms).
- 1.5x baseline: P95 ~ 380ms (cache on: ~260ms), P99 ~ 780ms (cache on: ~520ms).
- 3x baseline: P95 degrades to ~650ms (cache on: ~420ms), P99 ~1.2s (cache on: ~760ms).

Notes: caching effectiveness depends on prompt reuse; if your sessions are highly unique, expect less benefit. Also our continuous-batching window will trade off latency for throughput — we can set a tighter max-batching latency target for the hot lane.

2) Rough unit economics (illustrative; final numbers will be in the workbook & commercial sheet):
- H100-80 (hot lane, premium SLA): ~$95 per 1M tokens served (low-latency, minimal quantization).
- A100-80 quantized (good latency/cost balance): ~$42 per 1M tokens (depending on quantization level and batch efficiency).
- L4-class batch (embeddings, quantized): ~$7–$12 per 1M tokens equivalent (embeddings measured as per-embedding unit; batching has large effect).

3) Reservation/burst mechanics:
- Burst credits: typically included as a contracted burst pool (pre-authorized capacity your account can draw) — usage above committed baseline billed at pre-agreed overage rates. We can structure bursts as prepaid credits or true metered overage depending on your procurement preference.
- Regional outages & failover: Redwood Dedicated supports cross-region failover for enterprise customers — failover takes application-level configuration. In a committed-reservation plan we guarantee priority scheduling in the primary region; cross-region fallback is supported but may require additional reserved capacity in the target region to meet strict SLA guarantees.

Next steps: I'll populate the reserved_capacity_workbook with numbers using your token distribution (220/180) and two scenarios: conservative (2x headroom) and aggressive (3x headroom with larger burst pool). I included links to a draft workbook at: https://redwood.app/drive/Orion-RFI-2026.

cc'ing Laura and Ben to loop in commercial/pricing and to coordinate the workshop.

Best,
Dev Patel
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
